precepts.text: Ye are my brethren, ye are my bones and my flesh; further proof that bone and flesh speaks of kindred.
precepts.point: Laban said unto Jacob, Surely thou art my bone and my flesh. In the scriptures that phrase means we are family; Jacob abode with him a month, and Laban, because Jacob was his brother, asked what his wages should be.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
David reminded the elders of Judah who they were to him: “Ye are my brethren, ye are my bones and my flesh: wherefore then are ye the last to bring back the king?” He calls them brethren and bones and flesh in the same breath; the two mean the same thing.

Further proof that bone and flesh speaks of kindred. When Laban said to Jacob, “Surely thou art my bone and my flesh”, and then called him “my brother”, he was saying the same thing David said to Judah: you are my family.

precepts.text: Shimei came out cursing David, casting stones, and calling him a bloody man and a man of Belial as he fled Jerusalem.
precepts.point: Abishai and the sons of Zeruiah said Shimei should be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed, but David rebuked them as adversaries, asking whether any man should be put to death that day in Israel when he knew he was king. He swore Shimei would not die. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

precepts.why:
When king David came to Bahurim, Shimei the son of Gera, of the family of the house of Saul, “came forth, and cursed still as he came. And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.” He cried, “Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial”.

That was David in a low state, fleeing Jerusalem, surrounded by his mighty men, and Shimei cursed him to his face. Now the king was coming back, and the same Shimei hasted down with a thousand men of Benjamin and fell down before him at Jordan: “Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem”. He confessed, “For thy servant doth know that I have sinned”.

Abishai said, “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” But David rebuked the sons of Zeruiah as adversaries: “shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I am this day king over Israel?” He said to Shimei, “Thou shalt not die”, and swore it. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

precepts.text: The Most High set man's days at a hundred and twenty years.
precepts.point: A quarrel then arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

precepts.why:
“And the Lord said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.” The Most High set man’s days at a hundred and twenty years.

Barzillai the Gileadite was “a very aged man, even fourscore years old”. At eighty he asked, “How long have I to live, that I should go up with the king unto Jerusalem?” He could no longer taste what he ate or drank, nor hear “the voice of singing men and singing women”. He would go only a little way over Jordan, and asked to turn back, “that I may die in mine own city, and be buried by the grave of my father and of my mother.”

Man’s days were set at a hundred and twenty years, yet at fourscore Barzillai was already very aged and ready to die.

precepts.text: The days of our years are threescore and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore years; a man is very aged at seventy and eighty.
precepts.point: A quarrel then arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

precepts.why:
“The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.” A man is very aged at seventy and eighty.

Barzillai was fourscore, the span given by reason of strength, and his strength was labour and sorrow: “can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women?” He would not be a burden to the king, so he sent Chimham over with David in his place, and the king kissed him and blessed him, and he returned unto his own place.

precepts.text: Eleazar was a very aged man, being fourscore years and ten; the Lord kept cutting our lifespan down because of sin.
precepts.point: A quarrel then arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

precepts.why:
Eleazar said, “it becometh not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, whereby many young persons might think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, were now gone to a strange religion”. Eleazar was a very aged man, being fourscore years and ten.

Like Barzillai at fourscore, Eleazar at fourscore and ten is counted very aged, far short of the hundred and twenty years the Most High first set. The Lord kept cutting our lifespan down because of sin.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: Joab came into the house and told David he had shamed the faces of all his servants who had saved his life and the lives of his sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, because he loved his enemies and hated his friends. Joab said if Absalom had lived and all of them had died, it would have pleased David well. No one else could speak to the king this way, but Joab knew David's skeletons.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: Joab charged David to arise and speak comfortably unto his servants, swearing that if he did not, not one man would tarry with him that night, and that would be worse than all the evil that had befallen him from his youth. Then the king arose and sat in the gate, and all the people came before him.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: All the tribes of Israel were at strife, saying the king had saved them from the Philistines and their enemies but had fled the land because of Absalom, who was now dead, so why did they say nothing about bringing the king back.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests to speak to the elders of Judah, asking why they were the last to bring the king back when they were his brethren, his bone and his flesh. He told Amasa that he would make him captain of the host in the room of Joab.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: David bowed the heart of all the men of Judah as the heart of one man, so they sent word for him to return with all his servants, and the king came again to Jordan while Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and conduct him over.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, having neither dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until he returned in peace, showing his mourning for David.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: When asked why he had not gone with the king, Mephibosheth said his servant Ziba had deceived him and slandered him, since Mephibosheth was lame and could not saddle his own beast. He acknowledged that all his father's house were dead men before the king, yet David had set him to eat at his own table, so he had no further right to cry to the king.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: David told him to speak no more of the matter and said that he and Ziba should divide the land. Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take it all, for it was enough that his lord the king had come again in peace to his own house.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: Barzillai the Gileadite, a very aged man of fourscore years, came down from Rogelim to conduct the king over Jordan, having provided the king with sustenance at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

points: When David invited him to come and be fed in Jerusalem, Barzillai asked how long he had to live that he should go up, saying at eighty years old he could no longer discern the taste of what he ate or drank nor hear the voice of singing men and women, so he would only go a little way over and asked to return and die in his own city by his parents' grave. He sent Chimham in his place, and the king kissed and blessed Barzillai, who returned to his own place.
